sections.skill: Calculate card fees and compare balance transfers, 0% APR offers, and deferred interest

questions.prompt: Nia moves a $4,000 balance at 22% APR to a new card with 0% APR for 15 months and a 3% balance transfer fee. What is the fee?
questions.intro: A balance transfer moves debt from one card to another, often to get a low promotional APR. Most transfers charge a fee, commonly 3% to 5% of the amount moved. The low rate lasts only for the promotional period.
questions.topic: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers
sources: CFPB (Understanding special promotional financing offers): With deferred interest, if the promotional balance is not paid in full by the end of the period, interest is charged back to the purchase date. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/how-understand-special-promotional-financing-offers-credit-cards/)

questions.prompt: Rough estimate: leaving $4,000 at 22% APR for 15 months, assuming the balance stayed at $4,000, would cost about $1,100 in interest. A transfer costs a $120 fee at 0% APR. About how much does the transfer save if Nia pays it off within 15 months?
questions.intro: Compare the cost of staying with the cost of transferring: interest avoided minus the transfer fee. Holding the balance constant gives only a rough estimate; if she pays it down, the interest avoided is smaller.
questions.feedback: $1,100 − $120 = $980 saved (rough), if the balance is paid off during the 0% period.
questions.topic: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers
sources: CFPB (Understanding special promotional financing offers): With deferred interest, if the promotional balance is not paid in full by the end of the period, interest is charged back to the purchase date. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/how-understand-special-promotional-financing-offers-credit-cards/)

questions.prompt: Nia's 0% transfer period ends in 15 months. What happens to any balance left after that?

choices.text: It is forgiven by the card issuer
It stays at 0% forever
It moves back to the old card automatically at its old rate
It starts being charged the card's regular APR

questions.correct_answer: It starts being charged the card's regular APR
questions.intro: A genuine introductory 0% APR charges no interest during the promotion. After it ends, the remaining balance is charged the regular APR going forward.
questions.feedback: Remaining balances start accruing interest at the regular rate after the promotion.
questions.topic: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers

misconceptions.B: Ignores the end of the promotion

sources: CFPB (Understanding special promotional financing offers): With deferred interest, if the promotional balance is not paid in full by the end of the period, interest is charged back to the purchase date. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/how-understand-special-promotional-financing-offers-credit-cards/)

questions.prompt: A store card says "No interest if paid in full within 12 months" on a $1,200 TV. This is deferred interest. Ana pays $1,190 by the deadline. What happens?

choices.text: She can owe all interest since the purchase date
She pays interest only on the remaining $10
Nothing is charged, since she paid almost all of it
The store refunds her payments

questions.correct_answer: She can owe all interest since the purchase date
questions.intro: Deferred interest is different from a true 0% APR. Interest builds up in the background from the purchase date. If the full promotional balance is not paid by the deadline, all of that interest can be charged at once.
questions.feedback: Missing full payoff by even $10 can trigger interest back to the purchase date.
questions.topic: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers

misconceptions.B: Treats it like a true 0% APR

questions.intro: Some cards charge a foreign transaction fee, often about 3%, on purchases made in another currency or processed abroad. Other cards charge none.

questions.prompt: What does "0% APR for 12 months" mean on a new card?

choices.text: No payments of any kind are required for 12 months
The card has no fees ever
No interest on qualifying balances for 12 months
Interest is charged only after 12 years

questions.correct_answer: No interest on qualifying balances for 12 months
questions.intro: A 0% introductory APR means no interest during the promotion. Minimum payments are still required each month.
questions.feedback: Minimum payments are still required; only the interest is 0%.

questions.prompt: Which fees would a cardholder most likely avoid if she always pays on time and makes no purchases in foreign currency or processed by foreign merchants (in person or online)?

choices.text: Every fee, including the annual fee
Interest on balances carried over
Balance transfer fees when transferring
Late fees and foreign transaction fees

questions.correct_answer: Late fees and foreign transaction fees
questions.intro: Foreign transaction fees can apply without leaving the country: an online purchase from a foreign merchant or in a foreign currency can trigger one.
questions.feedback: Paying on time avoids late fees; avoiding foreign-currency or foreign-processed purchases avoids foreign transaction fees.

sections.skill: Deferred interest versus a true 0% intro APR

questions.prompt: Card X offers a true 0% intro APR for 12 months. Card Y offers deferred interest for 12 months at 26.99%. Both have $1,200 purchases and $100 left at month 12. Which statement is TRUE?

choices.text: Only Card Y can charge a year of back interest
Both charge the same interest
Card Y charges less because its rate is deferred
Neither charges any interest ever

questions.correct_answer: Only Card Y can charge a year of back interest
questions.intro: True 0% APR: interest starts only on what remains after the promotion ends. Deferred interest: interest builds from the purchase date and is charged in full if any promotional balance remains at the deadline.
questions.feedback: True 0% never charges back interest; deferred interest does.
questions.topic: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers

questions.prompt: Ana's deferred-interest statements show $230 of "accrued interest" building over 12 months. She leaves $10 unpaid at the deadline. How much interest is likely added?
questions.intro: Deferred interest is all-or-nothing: if any promotional balance remains at the deadline, all the accrued interest can be added.
questions.feedback: All of the deferred interest can be charged when any promotional balance remains.
questions.topic: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers

questions.intro: With deferred interest, minimum payments are often too small to pay the promotional balance in time. Divide the balance by the months available.

questions.prompt: Which phrase in an ad signals DEFERRED interest rather than a true 0% APR?

choices.text: "No interest if paid in full within 12 months"
"0% intro APR on purchases for 12 months"
"Regular APR 21.99%"
"No annual fee"

questions.correct_answer: "No interest if paid in full within 12 months"
questions.intro: "If paid in full" wording usually means deferred interest. "0% intro APR" usually means interest-free during the period.
questions.feedback: "If paid in full" is the hallmark of deferred interest.
questions.topic: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers
sources: CFPB (Understanding special promotional financing offers): With deferred interest, if the promotional balance is not paid in full by the end of the period, interest is charged back to the purchase date. questions.prompt: Why are minimum payments on deferred-interest plans risky?

choices.text: They pay off the promo balance before the end date
They cancel the promotion as soon as one is made
They stop interest from ever being charged
They may not clear the promo balance in time

questions.correct_answer: They may not clear the promo balance in time
questions.intro: Minimum payments are set as a small share of the balance, not as the amount needed to pay off a promotional balance by its deadline.
questions.feedback: A small minimum can leave a balance at the deadline, triggering all the back interest.
questions.topic: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers

misconceptions.A: Assumes minimum payments are timed to the promotion
misconceptions.C: Believes paying something prevents deferred interest

questions.prompt: Which habit can undo the benefit of a balance transfer?

choices.text: Paying more than the minimum
Setting up autopay
Running up new charges on the old card
Tracking the date the promotion ends each month

questions.correct_answer: Running up new charges on the old card
questions.intro: A balance transfer only helps if the debt shrinks. New spending can rebuild the old balance while the transferred one is being paid.
questions.feedback: New charges can leave two balances instead of one.

questions.prompt: A transfer offer: 0% for 6 months, 5% fee. Debt: $2,000 at 18% APR. Rough estimate, assuming the balance stays at $2,000: about how much would 6 months at 18% cost (simple), and is the transfer worth it?

choices.text: About $360 vs $100; never worth it
About $18 vs $100; always worth it
About $180 vs $10; worth it
About $180 in interest vs a $100 fee; worth it if paid off in 6 months

questions.correct_answer: About $180 in interest vs a $100 fee; worth it if paid off in 6 months
questions.intro: Compare the interest avoided during the promotion with the transfer fee. A constant balance gives only a rough comparison.
questions.feedback: $2,000 × 0.18 × 0.5 = $180 vs 5% × $2,000 = $100: saves about $80, if paid off in time.

questions.prompt: Which fact should Nia check BEFORE transferring?

choices.text: Only the new card's credit limit
Only the rewards points
The fee, promo length, and later APR
Only whether the new card has an annual fee

questions.correct_answer: The fee, promo length, and later APR
questions.intro: Three numbers decide whether a transfer saves money: the transfer fee, how long the promotional rate lasts, and the rate afterward.
questions.feedback: Those three numbers decide whether a transfer saves money.
questions.topic: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers

misconceptions.D: Misses the transfer fee and promo length
